opus-5.5.text:
I think the home is one of the hardest environments you could ask a robot to work in, and the reasons are a bit counterintuitive, because we take it for granted as humans.

The first thing is diversity. In a factory you can design the environment around the robot: fixed lighting, parts in known positions, the same motion repeated thousands of times. A home is the opposite. Every kitchen is laid out differently, every family keeps things in different places, and even the same house changes day to day. A cup ends up on the sofa, a towel is draped over a chair, a kid leaves toys on the floor. The robot can't assume a fixed world. It has to generalize to situations it has never seen.

The second is the objects themselves. Household manipulation involves a huge long tail: deformable things like clothes and bedsheets, transparent or reflective things like glasses, fragile things, articulated things like drawers and fridge doors, food that is slippery or squishy. Each of these is a research problem on its own, and in a home you face all of them within ten minutes of chores.

Third, the tasks are long-horizon and loosely specified. "Tidy the living room" isn't one motion. It's dozens of decisions: what counts as messy, where each item belongs, what order makes sense. A lot of that depends on the preferences of the particular person living there, which you can't hard-code.

Fourth, and maybe most important, is the bar for reliability and safety. People are physically close to the robot. There are children, elderly people, pets. A system that succeeds 90% of the time sounds good in a paper, but if it drops a plate or bumps into a toddler one time in ten, nobody will keep it in their house. Consumers have very little tolerance for failure in their personal space, and they also expect it to be affordable and quiet and not need an engineer to babysit it.

So when you put it all together, open-ended environments, a long tail of objects, vague long tasks, and near-zero tolerance for mistakes, the home really becomes the ultimate test of general-purpose physical intelligence. That's also why I find it so exciting. If you can make robots genuinely useful at home, you've basically solved most of the core problems in embodied AI along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says homes vary in layout and change day to day, so robots cannot assume a fixed world and must generalize to situations they have never seen.

r002.rationale: It describes household tasks such as tidying as long-horizon and loosely specified, involving dozens of decisions about items, destinations, and task order.

fable-5.1.text:
Because a home is the opposite of a factory. In a factory you control everything: the lighting is fixed, the parts arrive in the same orientation, the floor is clean, and if something goes wrong there's a cage and an emergency stop. A home has none of that. Every apartment is laid out differently, the furniture gets moved, the lighting changes from morning to night, there's a cat walking through, a child leaving toys on the floor. The robot has to deal with an open-ended, constantly shifting environment, and it can't just stop and wait for an engineer.

Then there's the objects themselves. In a warehouse you might handle a few hundred SKUs. In a home it's effectively infinite: a wine glass, a wet sponge, a crumpled shirt, a half-full cup of coffee, a bag of chips. Many of them are deformable, transparent, fragile, or all three. Folding laundry alone is a problem that has humbled a lot of very good labs, because fabric has no fixed shape and you can't model it the way you model a rigid box.

And the stakes are different. The robot is operating inches from people, sometimes elderly people or kids. A mistake isn't a scratched part, it's a knocked-over grandmother or a broken heirloom. So the tolerance for error is extremely low, while the variability is extremely high. That combination is the hardest thing in robotics.

The last piece is cost and expectations. A family won't pay industrial prices, and they won't accept a robot that works 90 percent of the time. If your dishwasher failed one load in ten you'd throw it out. So you need near-perfect reliability, in an uncontrolled environment, at consumer cost. That's why I think of the home as the real exam for the field. If you can make something genuinely useful there, you've probably solved most of the hard problems everywhere else too.

r001.rationale: It says every apartment is laid out differently and that homes are open-ended, constantly shifting environments the robot must handle, conveying the need to cope with unfamiliar variation.

r002.rationale: It describes varied household objects and difficult laundry, but does not identify an open-ended variety of household tasks or explain that this creates high action complexity.

astra-6.text:
Because a home is built around people, and people don’t keep everything in exactly the same place. A chair moves, clothes end up on the floor, a child or a pet suddenly crosses the room. The robot has to cope with all of that safely, without asking the household to reorganize itself around the machine.

And even a simple request like “clear the table” involves a lot of judgment. What should go in the sink? What should stay? Is that cup empty, or could it spill? You need perception, physical dexterity, and an understanding of what the person actually wants, all working together. Doing something once is one challenge; doing it reliably every day in different homes is a much harder one.

r001.rationale: The response says robots must cope reliably in “different homes,” but does not explain that variation between homes requires generalizing to unfamiliar environments.

r002.rationale: It describes the judgment and dexterity involved in clearing a table, but does not identify the open-ended variety of household tasks as the source of high action complexity.

sol-6.1.text: Because a home is a very unstructured environment. In a factory, you can control where things are, what the robot handles, and how the task is performed. In a household, every room is different, objects move around, and people may interrupt you at any moment. Even something that sounds simple, like clearing a table, involves recognizing objects, handling fragile items, and understanding what should go where. And the robot has to do all of that safely around people, reliably enough that it actually saves them effort. That combination makes household use very demanding.

r001.rationale: The response says rooms and object arrangements differ, but does not explain that robots must generalize to unfamiliar homes or environments.

r002.rationale: It describes several steps involved in clearing a table, but does not identify the open-ended variety of household tasks as the source of robots’ high action complexity.
